| **8.1.1** Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for restricting function-level and data-specific access based on consumer permissions and resource attributes. | L1 | pass | test `[ASVS-8.1.1]`<br>doc [docs/security/authorization.md](../../../docs/security/authorization.md)<br>doc [modules/core-authz/README.md](../../../modules/core-authz/README.md)<br>doc [docs/adr/0014-authorisation-model-and-dependency-direction.md](../../../docs/adr/0014-authorisation-model-and-dependency-direction.md)<br>doc [docs/adr/0005-deny-by-default-before-authz.md](../../../docs/adr/0005-deny-by-default-before-authz.md) | docs/security/authorization.md is the single place: the two checks (route permission, then the service with the resource), one table of every route with its permission, the rules on one resource (own sessions, tokens, inbox items, pending accounts, role assignment) and the rules that hold for Admin too. The route table is generated from the live registry and a tagged test fails when the page differs from it. The mechanics of a decision stay in the core.authz README and the two ADRs, which the page links. Resource policies exist as a mechanism and are tested with a fixture module; the page gets their rows when the registry modules add real ones (M7). M5 sprint 3 added six routes (the administrator's user list, one user, the roles and tokens of a user, deactivation, and the permissions of a role); they are in the generated table and the same test fails for any that is missing. M5 sprint 4 added GET /permissions (core.authz.role.read) and GET /account/permissions (core.authz.account.read, the caller's own permissions, limited to the scopes of an access token); both are in the generated table and in the walker. `GET /inbox/stream` (sprint 4, ADR-0028) is a self-service route in the walker: it has no id in the request, so there is no other person's stream to open (apps/server/src/inbox-stream-routes.test.ts: a user id in the address changes nothing), it needs `core.notifications.inbox.read` on the route and again in the service, an access token needs the scope, and every heartbeat re-checks the permission and the credentials. |

The resource-policy mechanism is tested with a fixture module; the real provider and service policies arrive in M7. This is sampling per service, not a systematic IDOR sweep. |
| **8.2.3** Verify that the application ensures that field-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific fields to mitigate broken object property level authorization (BOPLA). | L2 | pass | test `[ASVS-8.2.3]`<br>doc [docs/security/authorization.md](../../../docs/security/authorization.md)<br>code [apps/server/src/response-fields.test.ts](../../../apps/server/src/response-fields.test.ts)<br>code [modules/core-identity/validation.ts](../../../modules/core-identity/validation.ts) | Scorpion has no field-level permission engine, by decision (M4b Decision 9); field access is kept by construction. Read side: every route returns one fixed response schema, and the tagged walker reads the response schema of every route of the live registry at any depth (arrays, unions, optionals, references) and fails on secretHash, passwordHash, tokenHash, clientSecret, secret, password or token, with the two one-time token responses (token create and rotate) as the only named exceptions; a planted violation is proved to be named. The audit of every response schema found no such field, and a further test in the same file checks the declared event payloads. Write side: every request body is a strict Zod object, so status, roles, userId or any unknown field is a 422, and status and roles change only through their own permissioned routes. Not shown: that a real response holds only what its schema declares (no step validates a response body; services build named fields, and the route tests for tokens, secrets, settings and the audit trail read real responses; docs/backlog.md schedules a check in the contract tests), that a free-form value such as a setting holds no secret-named key, and that a field is right for its reader. That is a review of the tables in docs/security/authorization.md against each schema, not something a test decides, and there is no per-role projection: two readers of one route see the same fields. |
| **8.3.1** Verify that the application enforces authorization rules at a trusted service layer and doesn't rely on controls that an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript. | L1 | pass | test `[ASVS-8.3.1]`<br>code [apps/server/src/pipeline/authorize.ts](../../../apps/server/src/pipeline/authorize.ts)<br>code [modules/core-authz/service/authz.ts](../../../modules/core-authz/service/authz.ts) | Authorization runs on the server in the pipeline and again in the service (ctx.authz.require); roles sent by a client are ignored (ADR-0014). Navigation hiding in the UI is cosmetic: the catch-all route of the web app opens a page only when the server lists it for the caller (GET /ui/navigation), and a public page must be named in PUBLIC_PAGES with a reason (apps/server/src/ui-routes.test.ts). M5 sprint 2 added two public routes, GET /auth/oidc/providers (id, display name and icon hash only) and GET /bootstrap/status (one boolean), each with its reason and in the generated route table of docs/security/authorization.md, and the sign-in, registration, recovery and first-admin pages; the profile page needs core.identity.profile.read. The page walker in apps/server/src/ui-navigation-routes.test.ts shows a plain User only the profile and public pages, and apps/web/e2e/navigation.spec.ts finds nothing of the administration in their navigation. The administration pages of M5 sprint 3 (users, pending approvals, roles, settings) are registered with a permission, so the same list gives a plain User none of them and the catch-all route answers their paths with 403 (apps/web/e2e/admin.spec.ts). |
